## 2 Related Works

We highlight the most relevant prior work here and defer a more detailed discussion to Appendix B.

Detecting and Quantifying Steganographic Reasoning. Existing formalisms define steganography in terms of statistical (Cachin, 2004) or computational (Hopper et al., 2002) indistinguishability between steganographic and benign signal. Accordingly, standard detection methods work by comparing the distribution of suspected text to that of known reference distribution, using either hand-crafted statistical features or learned representations derived from machine learning models (Wu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022; Zou et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023). In the context of LLMs, this paradigm has also been operationalised through LLM-as-a-judge approaches, where a model evaluates whether generated text appears “suspicious” (Zolkowski et al., 2025) or “illegible” (Jose, 2025; Emmons et al., 2025). However, such methods typically rely on access to representative samples from the reference benign distribution. The challenge of applying this paradigm to the analysis of LLM reasoning and communication is that obtaining such samples, and ensuring they are indeed benign, is difficult. Thus, our framework sidesteps this requirement by asking whether access to the signal changes an agent’s decisions, rather than whether the signal deviates from a reference distribution.

#### Steganographic Capabilities in Language Models.

Recent work has investigated the emergence of steganographic capabilities in frontier LLMs. One line of research studies steganographic communication, where one model embeds hidden information in benign-looking text that other models can later decode. Several works show that explicit steganographic schemes can be induced via prompting or fine-tuning (Roger and Greenblatt, 2023; Zolkowski et al., 2025; Motwani et al., 2025), or more organically through training against an overseer (Mathew et al., 2024). A related but distinct phenomenon is steganographic (encoded) reasoning11 1 In this work, we use the terms ‘steganographic’ and ‘encoded’ reasoning interchangeably., where a model produces reasoning traces that are unintelligible to a monitor but remain useful to the model itself (Roger and Greenblatt, 2023; Skaf et al., 2025). Prior works show that current LLMs can reason using simple encoding schemes when instructed to do so, though this ability degrades for more complex generations (Zolkowski et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). In addition, Schoen et al. (2025); Jose (2025) showed that frontier reasoning models exhibit signs of non-standard language use in their CoT, increasing the urgency of research towards better understanding and counteracting steganographic reasoning.

## 3 Generalised $\mathcal{V}$ -Information

In order to formally describe our decision-theoretic treatment of steganography, we require a notion of usable information: a measure of how much an auxiliary variable $Z$ improves decision-making for a given class of agents. For this purpose, we adapt and extend the $\mathcal{V}$ -information framework of Xu et al. (2020). We provide a brief overview below and defer a more formal treatment to Appendix C.

### 3.1 Setup and Notation

Let $X\in\mathcal{X}$ be some input, $Y\in\mathcal{Y}$ be the corresponding output, and let $Z\in\mathcal{Z}$ be some auxiliary variable, the ‘usefulness’ of which we aim to quantify.

A decoder $d$ is a mapping $d:\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{aud}}\times(\mathcal{Z}\cup\varnothing)\to\mathcal{C}$ from available information to an element of an output space $\mathcal{C}$ . We consider two decoding regimes: decoding directly from the input via $d[X]$ , and decoding from both the input and $Z$ via $d[X,Z]$ . We use $\mathcal{V}$ to denote a family of admissible decoders. We generally presume these decoders to be capacity and compute constrained.

### 3.2 Predictive $\mathcal{V}$ -Information

A central theme of $\mathcal{V}$ -information is that how information is represented can matter as much as whether it exists. For example, encrypting a text input $X$ may not remove the Shannon information it contains about a label $Y$ , yet it can make predicting $Y$ much harder for any predictor family with capacity and compute constraints. This motivates the concept of usable information: information measured relative to the decoding capabilities of the predictor family.

Following Xu et al. (2020), let $\Omega$ be a set of all decoders the output space $\mathcal{C}$ is the space of probability measures over $\mathcal{Y}$ (i.e., decoders that map provided information to distributions over $\mathcal{Y}$ ), and let $\mathcal{V}\subseteq\Omega$ be a predictive family satisfying optional ignorance (i.e., the family contains predictors that can effectively ignore the provided side information if needed). Define the predictive $\mathcal{V}$ -entropy under log loss as

$$ \displaystyle H_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X) \displaystyle=\inf_{d\in\mathcal{V}}\;\mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\big[-\log d[X](Y)\big], \displaystyle H_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X,Z) \displaystyle=\inf_{d\in\mathcal{V}}\;\mathbb{E}_{X,Y,Z}\big[-\log d[X,Z](Y)\big], $$

where $d[x]\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})$ denotes the probability measure over $\mathcal{Y}$ chosen based on the received side information $x$ . Further, $d[x](y)\in R$ is the value of density evaluated at $y\in\mathcal{Y}$ . The (conditional) predictive $\mathcal{V}$ -information provided by $Z$ about $Y$ given $X$ is then defined as the improvement in best achievable log loss:

$$ I_{\mathcal{V}}(Z\to Y\mid X)\;=\;H_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X)\;-\;H_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X,Z). $$

### 3.3 Generalised $\mathcal{V}$ -information (GVI)

While $\mathcal{V}$ -information provides a principled measure of usable information, it requires each decoder to output a full predictive distribution, making it challenging to apply in practice. For example, in the context of LLMs, cross-model comparisons based on log-probabilities are known to be brittle, hard to interpret, and sensitive to stylistic differences between models (Li et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2024). Moreover, in AI oversight and many other settings, we care about metrics like accuracy or recall rather than log loss. Therefore we adopt a utilitarian view of information (Zhao et al., 2021; Ermon, 2022) and use a utility-based generalization of $\mathcal{V}$ -information called generalised $\mathcal{V}$ -information, which allows us to evaluate responses using a utility function $u:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{R}$ , tailored to alternative output spaces $\mathcal{C}$ . Intuitively, $u(y,c)$ measures the utility for a decoder $d(\cdot)$ outputting response $c$ when the true target is $y$ .

Given a decoder family $\mathcal{V}$ and utility $u$ , we define the maximal achievable expected utility when decoding based on $X$ and $(X,Z)$ as:

$$ \displaystyle U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X) \displaystyle=\sup_{d\in\mathcal{V}}\;\mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\big[u(Y,d[X])\big], \displaystyle U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X,Z) \displaystyle=\sup_{d\in\mathcal{V}}\;\mathbb{E}_{X,Y,Z}\big[u(Y,d[X,Z])\big]. $$

The generalised $\mathcal{V}$ -information (GVI) is then the gain in utility achievable by the best decoders in $\mathcal{V}$ by additionally observing $Z$ :

$$ I^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Z\to Y\mid X)\;=\;U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X,Z)\;-\;U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X). $$

Similar to $\mathcal{V}$ -information, GVI turns “information” into a measure of strategic advantage: $Z$ is valuable only insofar as it enables some decoder in $\mathcal{V}$ to achieve higher task utility. $Z$ can therefore be information-rich in the Shannon sense, yet have zero GVI if no decoder in $\mathcal{V}$ can exploit it (e.g., if $Z$ is in French and decoders in $\mathcal{V}$ only understand English).

The main usefulness of GVI is that it allows a practitioner to measure usable information with respect to any utility function of her choice. For example, if one is interested in evaluating how helpful $Z$ is in terms of performing some task $X$ better, this can be measured with GVI using task accuracy as the utility function.22 2 Formally, if $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{Y}$ (i.e., the space of task answers) and $u(y,c)=\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}=c]$ , then $I^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Z\rightarrow Y\mid X)$ measures the expected increase in task accuracy attributable to having access to $Z$ for the best decoder in $\mathcal{V}$ . Furthermore, GVI is a strict generalization of predictive $\mathcal{V}$ -Information. Specifically, if we set $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})$ , i.e., the space of predictive distributions over $Y$ , and $u(y,c)=\log c(y)$ , then the induced $I^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Z\rightarrow Y\mid X)$ reduces to predictive $\mathcal{V}$ -information.

## 4 Decision-Theoretic Formalisation of Steganography

Equipped with the generalised $\mathcal{V}$ -information, we now introduce our decision-theoretic formalism for steganography.

### 4.1 From Monitoring Messages to Monitoring Actions

Consider the classical steganographic setting: a Sender transmits a message $Z$ to a Receiver over a public channel monitored by an Auditor.33 3 The Auditor is analogous to the warden in classical formulations (Simmons, 1984). In the standard model, the Auditor must judge whether $Z$ is steganographic based solely on the message itself and knowledge of a benign covertext distribution (Cachin, 2004; Hopper et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2019a). This standard model has two clear shortcomings: it makes detection impossible when covertext distributions are unknown (as with LLM reasoning) or when the steganographic scheme is perfectly secure and $Z$ is statistically indistinguishable from the covertext.

However, steganography is generally not employed for its own sake, but is often used in an instrumental way to achieve some strategic objective. For example, in Simmons’ original formulation, prisoners goal in using steganographic communication is to coordinate an escape plan (Simmons, 1984). In the LLM setting, the LLM’s goal in using steganography is to avoid being penalised for using prohibited reasoning that helps the model perform better on some task (Skaf et al., 2025). Because steganographic content is instrumental, its value must ultimately manifest through the Receiver’s actions.

This motivates our extension: we allow the Auditor to observe not only $Z$ , but also how $Z$ affects the Receiver’s downstream decisions. This creates an alternative detection surface—even if the Auditor cannot decode $Z$ directly, it may infer hidden content by observing its downstream effects.

To capture such effects, we adopt a comparative approach: we allow the Auditor to evaluate not only the actions of the Receiver, but also of a trusted Sentinel—an agent with comparable capabilities, but without knowledge of the encoding scheme used by the Sender and Receiver. Then, any systematic difference in performance between the Receiver and the Sentinel in response to the message reflects the effect of the encoded information, available only to the Receiver. In the language of usable information, a steganographic message induces an asymmetry between agents: it contains more usable information for the Receiver than for the Sentinel. This asymmetry manifests through their actions and can be quantified using generalised $\mathcal{V}$ -information (see Section 4.3). Thus, monitoring the gap in the generalised $\mathcal{V}$ -information between the Receiver and the Sentinel can allow the Auditor to detect the presence of steganographic information.

### 4.2 Setup and Notation

We visualise our setup in Figure 2. We make a distinction between a generation context $X^{\mathrm{gen}}$ and an auditing context $X^{\mathrm{aud}}$ . Generation of (potentially) steganographic content happens within the generation context, while the analysis occurs within the auditing context.

Formally, upon observing $X^{\mathrm{gen}}\in\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{gen}}$ , the Sender generates a signal $Z\in\mathcal{Z}\sim P_{S}(Z\mid X^{\mathrm{gen}})$ . The Auditor specifies how $Z$ will be evaluated, by specifying an auditing task defined through the tuple $(X^{\mathrm{aud}},u,Y)$ . Both the Receiver and Sentinel observe $X^{\mathrm{aud}}$ and (optionally) $Z$ , and must produce a response $c\in\mathcal{C}$ . The responses (decisions) are scored against ground truth $Y$ using utility $u:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{R}$ .

This maps directly onto the GVI framework of Section 3: $X^{\mathrm{aud}}$ plays the role of the input $X$ , and the signal $Z$ is the auxiliary variable whose usefulness we wish to quantify. The Receiver and Sentinel are distinguished by their decoder families $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{rec}}$ and $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{sen}}$ , which may differ due to access to keys, prior knowledge, or computational resources.

### 4.3 Steganographic Gap

Given this setup, we now proceed to quantify the strength of steganography using the generalised $\mathcal{V}$ -information.

The Receiver-usable information of $Z$ quantifies the utility gain (under $u$ ) that the best decoder in Receiver’s decoding class $V_{\text{rec}}$ can obtain from observing $Z$ , relative to decoding from $X$ alone.

$$ \displaystyle I_{\mathrm{rec}}(Z\!\to\!Y)\; \displaystyle=\;I^{u}_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{rec}}}(Z\!\to\!Y\mid X^{\text{aud}}) \displaystyle=\;U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{rec}}}(Y\mid X^{\text{aud}},Z)\;-\;U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{rec}}}(Y\mid X^{\text{aud}}). $$

The Sentinel-usable information $I_{\mathrm{sen}}(Z\!\to\!Y)=I^{u}_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{sen}}}(Z\!\to\!Y\mid X^{\text{aud}})$ is defined analogously. The steganographic gap is then defined as

$$ \Delta_{\mathrm{steg}}(Z)\;=\;I_{\mathrm{rec}}(Z\!\to\!Y)\;-\;I_{\mathrm{sen}}(Z\!\to\!Y). $$

In this framework, signal $Z$ is steganographic if it induces a positive steganographic gap, which indicates that there is some information encoded in $Z$ that is operationally accessible to $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{rec}}$ but comparatively inaccessible to $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{sen}}$ for the objective $(Y,u)$ .

$\Delta_{\text{steg}}(Z)$ inherits the units of the utility function $u$ . For example, when $u$ is accuracy utility, $I_{\text{rec}}$ and $I_{\text{sen}}$ are improvements in accuracy from access to $Z$ , and $-100\leq\Delta_{\text{steg}}(Z)\leq 100$ is measured in percentage points of accuracy advantage (rather than bits per token). To avoid this confusion related to units, we define and use normalised steganographic gap which is dimensionless and has a maximum value of $1$ , making it easier to interpret.

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{steg}}(Z)\;=\;\frac{\Delta_{\text{steg}}(Z)}{I_{\text{rec}}(Z\!\to\!Y)}\;=\;1-\frac{I_{\text{sen}}(Z\!\to\!Y)}{I_{\text{rec}}(Z\!\to\!Y)}. $$

When $I_{\text{rec}}(Z\!\to\!Y)>0$ , and $\Delta_{\text{steg}}(Z)>0$ , $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{steg}}(Z)$ can be interpreted as the fraction of $Z$ ’s usable information that is accessible to the Receiver but not by the Sentinel.

### 4.4 Discussion

We conclude this section by discussing key properties of the proposed formalism, its relationship to existing approaches, and its scope of applicability. A formal treatment of the theoretical scope and limitations is given in Appendix E.

#### Dependence on Sentinel Capability and Auditing Task.

The steganographic gap depends explicitly on the decoder class $\mathcal{V}_{\text{sen}}$ . A reasoning trace may be steganographic with respect to one Sentinel but not another: a more capable Sentinel family may successfully decode information that a weaker one cannot, reducing or eliminating the gap. This captures the adversarial nature of steganography (also see Section 6.5). Note that defining steganography relative to a particular (class of) Sentinels is not unique to our framework. In the classical information-theoretic formalism, steganographic security is similarly defined relative to the assumed cover distribution and computational capabilities of the adversary, and changing these can change whether a given encoding scheme is considered secure.

The steganographic gap is also defined with respect to a specific auditing task. This reflects practical reality that steganography is typically employed to achieve specific adversarial goals—e.g., coordinating prohibited actions (Simmons, 1984)—and detection efforts are typically oriented around preventing these known threats. Defining steganography relative to an auditing objective reflects this reality: the Auditor’s task is not to detect hidden information in the abstract, but to prevent its use for particular harmful purposes, which are reflected in the choice of the auditing task (also see Section 6.4).

#### Scope and Assumptions.

Our decision-theoretic formalism works by examining the decisions that agents take upon receiving a potentially steganographic signal—an affordance that may not be available in all scenarios. In general, the framework may be applied in settings where three conditions hold:

- 1. Interceptability and Replayability: First, the signal $Z$ must be interceptable and replayable, so that it could be presented to both Receiver and Auditor independently.

- 2. Action recoverability: Second, it is important that the decoder’s response to $Z$ can be evaluated in a controlled setting, without committing to (potentially dangerous) irreversible real-world effects.

- 3. Temporal immediacy: Finally, we implicitly assume that steganographic content yields measurable effects within the auditing task’s evaluation horizon. If this does not hold, and the effects of the encoded signal only become apparent under future conditions, our framework would fail to capture these effects, and thus may fail to detect steganography.

All three conditions are satisfied in our primary setting of interest: auditing and monitoring reasoning in LLMs. Reasoning traces can generally be replayed to arbitrary models, model outputs are text, or tool calls, that generally can be evaluated in controlled environments (sandboxes) without real-world consequences, and single-turn reasoning provides immediate behavioural signal.

#### 4.4.1 Relationship to Existing Approaches

Classic Information-Theoretic Approach. Theoretically, our framework recovers classical information-theoretic security as a special case when the auditing task is binary detection, i.e., distinguishing steganographic signals from a cover distribution (see Appendix D). In practice, the two approaches are likely to complement each other. For instance, computationally cheap methods based on statistical distinguishability could provide initial screening, while our approach could be used in cases where more rigorous and targeted assessment is needed.

Anthropic’s Approach. Anthropic is the only frontier lab that has publicly reported performing evaluations to rule out encoded reasoning in LLMs (Anthropic, 2026, Section 6.4.2). Their approach is narrowly focused on ruling out any encoded reasoning learned by an LLM during RL training (Roger, 2025). They collect reasoning traces from the RL-trained model, paraphrase them with another LLM, and fine-tune the corresponding base model on both original and paraphrased traces; a performance gap between the two distilled models is taken as evidence of encoded reasoning. However, as noted by Roger (2025) themselves, both paraphrasing and distillation steps introduce confounders that make both positive and negative results difficult to interpret. Paraphrasing may fail to remove encoded content, since paraphrase-resistant steganographic schemes exist (Mathew et al., 2024; Perry et al., 2025), thus, yielding no gap despite encoded reasoning. Similarly, even if the original traces contained encoded content that was useful to the source model, the base model used for distillation may simply fail to acquire and use the corresponding encoding or decoding strategy from the finite distillation corpus. We may also get a spurious gap due to paraphraser removing legitimate reasoning steps, or due to paraphrased traces being less learnable due to some reason unrelated to encoded reasoning. More generally, this method confounds properties of the trace with properties of the paraphrasing and the distillation process. See Appendix A for a detailed critique of paraphrasing as a diagnostic tool for steganography, including a comparison with our approach.

## 5 Quantifying Steganographic Reasoning in LLMs

In this section, we show how our formalism can be applied to detect and quantify steganographic reasoning in LLMs. We focus on settings in which, under some generation context $X^{\text{gen}}$ (e.g., a task or a question requiring extensive reasoning), an LLM is suspected of using steganographic reasoning. In this setting, the Sender LLM acts as both the Sender and the Receiver: we interpret the model as communicating with itself through its reasoning trace $Z$ .44 4 This can be trivially extended to the case of steganographic communication between LLM agents by keeping the Sender and Receiver separate. This corresponds to a special case of our general framework in which the same agent both produces and exploits the steganographic signal. Since the LLM plays both roles, we refer to it as $R$ (for Receiver) to distinguish it from a trusted Sentinel LLM $S$ .

Our goal is to quantify the degree to which reasoning traces $Z$ generated by $R$ are steganographic with respect to an auditing task (specified via $(u,Y)$ c.f. Section 4.2). That is, we measure whether $Z$ contains information relevant to the auditing task that is usable by $R$ but not by the Sentinel $S$ .

We assume access to a dataset of generation tasks $\mathcal{T}^{\text{gen}}=\{T_{1}^{\text{gen}},\ldots,T_{n}^{\text{gen}}\}$ and corresponding auditing tasks $\mathcal{T}^{\text{aud}}=\{T_{1}^{\text{aud}},\ldots,T_{n}^{\text{aud}}\}$ , where each auditing task has a target $Y_{i}$ , and a utility function $u$ that is shared by all auditing tasks. The auditing task may coincide with the generation task, but need not—for instance, the generation task might be to solve a coding problem, while the auditing task tests whether the reasoning trace reveals information about bypassing certain checks.

To generate a reasoning trace $Z_{i}$ , we combine the generation task $T_{i}^{\text{gen}}$ with a generation prompt $p^{\text{gen}}$ ,55 5 We list all prompts used in Appendix G.3. forming the generation context $X_{i}^{\text{gen}}=[p^{\text{gen}};T_{i}^{\text{gen}}]$ . The reasoning trace is then sampled as $Z_{i}\sim R(\cdot\mid X_{i}^{\text{gen}})$ .

To evaluate utilities, we construct an auditing context $X_{i}^{\text{aud}}~=~[p^{\text{aud}};~T_{i}^{\text{aud}}]$ using the auditing task and an auditing prompt. We use two auditing prompts: when estimating baseline utility $U^{u}(Y\mid X^{\text{aud}})$ , we use $p^{\text{x-only}}$ ; when estimating $U^{u}(Y\mid X^{\text{aud}},Z)$ , we use $p^{\text{xz}}$ . Both prompts instruct the model to answer immediately without producing any intermediate reasoning. $p^{\text{xz}}$ additionally encourages the model to base its answer on the provided reasoning trace $Z$ . Both the Receiver $R$ and Sentinel $S$ are evaluated under identical prompts, ensuring a fair comparison. We estimate the Receiver-usable and Sentinel-usable information by replacing expectations with empirical averages, sampling multiple reasoning traces per task to reduce variance. Full details of the estimation procedure are provided in Appendix F.

## 6 Validating the Proposed Formalism

In this section, we empirically validate our formalism by showing that it aligns with typical notions of steganographic reasoning. Since current LLMs have only nascent steganographic capabilities (Zolkowski et al., 2025), we simulate steganographic reasoning using three methods of increasing realism: post-hoc ciphering, training with process supervision, and training to produce ciphered reasoning. Across all three methods, $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{steg}}$ behaves as expected: near zero when the decoding capabilities of Receiver and Sentinel are matched exactly, and approaching one as the information asymmetry grows. We note that as we are studying steganographic reasoning, the same LLM acts as both Sender and Receiver and is denoted as $R$ throughout this section.

### 6.1 $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\mathrm{steg}}$ Increases with Encoding Strength

Our first approach is motivated by prior work using ciphers as a proxy for steganographic reasoning (Guo et al., 2025). At the high-level, this approach works by selectively showing the Sentinel LLM $S$ a manually ciphered reasoning trace, while the Receiver LLM $R$ is shown the original (plaintext) reasoning trace, thus artificially creating controlled asymmetry in terms of usable information.

We draw generation tasks from GSM8k (Cobbe et al., 2021), MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), and CoinFlip (Skaf et al., 2025), where each sample constitutes one task. GSM8k consists of grade-school math word problems, MMLU-Pro is a challenging multiple-choice benchmark spanning diverse domains, and CoinFlip is a synthetic state-tracking task where the model must track the outcome of a sequence of coin flips given their relative outcomes. All three datasets were selected because chain-of-thought provides significant uplift (Sprague et al., 2025); this ensures that $I_{\text{rec}}(Z\to Y)>0$ , without which the steganographic gap would be trivially zero.

We use Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct as $R$ to generate reasoning traces $Z$ . See Appendix G.4 for the prompt used for this purpose and other relevant details. We set auditing task to be same as the generation task: predicting the correct answer for the given task (e.g., a question from GSM8k), with accuracy as the utility $u$ . When computing $U_{\mathcal{V}}^{u}(Y|X,Z)$ , both $R$ and $S$ receive the task; the difference lies in the reasoning trace— $R$ always observes the original, while $S$ receives a (possibly ciphered) version. We simulate varying degrees of steganography by independently applying a Rot13 encoding to each word in $Z$ with probability $p\in[0,1]$ , before presenting it to $S$ —interpolating between fully legible ( $p=0$ ) and fully ciphered ( $p=1$ ) traces. Since Rot13 leaves numerals unchanged, we verbalise mathematical expressions before encoding (see Appendix G.4 for details and ablations).

*Figure 3: Steganographic gap increases smoothly as higher portions of $Z$ are encoded using Rot13.*

As shown in Figure 3, the steganographic gap increases smoothly as the encoding probability $p$ increases. This validates the claim that $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{steg}}$ is sensitive to graded changes in encoding strength and can act as a quantitative measure. As one should expect, for Qwen-2.5-14B-Instruct as the Sentinel model, we have $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{steg}}=0$ for $p=0$ (corresponding to fully legible reasoning traces) and $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{steg}}=1$ for $p=1$ (corresponding to fully illegible reasoning traces). However, when using a weaker Sentinel (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct), we observe negative gaps at low encoding levels: the weaker model benefits from $Z$ even more than $R$ does, since it has lower baseline capabilities. Detailed accuracy breakdowns are provided in Appendix I.

### 6.2 $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\mathrm{steg}}$ Increases with Codebook Mismatch

In our second approach, we finetune models using reinforcement learning with a process-based reward on the CoinFlip task to reason using codewords (Skaf et al., 2025).

We train three policies. $\pi_{\text{no-stego}}$ is a baseline trained with task reward only. $\pi_{\text{mid-stego}}$ uses two codewords: Sun for Heads and Moon for Tails. $\pi_{\text{high-stego}}$ uses a larger codebook: Heads may be denoted by either Sun or East, and Tails by either Moon or West. The auditing task again coincides with the generation task: predicting the final state of the coin (Heads or Tails), with accuracy as the utility $u$ . We evaluate all pairwise combinations of policies, where one policy acts as the Receiver $R$ and another as the Sentinel $S$ .

### 6.3 $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\mathrm{steg}}$ Increases with Cipher Training

Inspired by Stickland and Korbak (2025), our third approach trains a model to directly produce cipher-encoded reasoning. We use the APPS backdoor task from Control Arena (Inglis et al., 2025) as our generation task. In this task, the model must solve a competitive programming problem while inserting a backdoor that activates on a specific input (the “secret”). Following Stickland and Korbak (2025), we fine-tune GPT-4.1 on reasoning traces encoded with a bigram substitution cipher, varying the number of training samples from 2000 to 6000. The fine-tuned model produces cipher-encoded traces $Z$ describing both program logic and the secret.

In this case, the auditing task differs from the generation task, and is to recover the secret input from the reasoning trace $Z$ . We measure whether the cipher-finetuned model (as $R$ ) has any advantage in extracting the secret from these traces, using extraction accuracy as the utility $u$ . We restrict evaluation to samples where the secret does not appear in plaintext within the trace.

As shown in Figure 4, $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{steg}}$ increases steadily as the number of fine-tuning samples increases—as the Receiver LLM $R$ becomes more proficient at hiding its reasoning using the cipher, $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{stego}}$ increases across all Sentinel models considered. This result also highlights the dependency of $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{steg}}$ on the Sentinel model. Curiously, GPT-4.1-based Sentinels show smaller gaps than GPT-5-based Sentinels, suggesting that Sentinels from the same model family as the Receiver (fine-tuned GPT-4.1) can partially decode its cipher-encoded traces, perhaps due to shared inductive biases or more strict guardrails in advanced models. See Appendix G.6 for full training details and further analysis.

*Figure 4: Steganographic gap increases with training: as the Receiver is fine-tuned on more cipher-encoded traces, its advantage over the Sentinel grows. Results are consistent across different Sentinels and seeds.*

### 6.4 $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\mathrm{steg}}$ Varies Across Auditing Tasks

As discussed in Section 4, the steganographic gap depends on the auditing objective $(Y,u,\mathcal{C})$ . The same reasoning trace may therefore be steganographic for one task while remaining fully accessible for another.

We illustrate this using Rot13 encoding on MMLU-Pro and GSM8k, exploiting the fact that Rot13 affects lexical content while leaving numbers unchanged. We construct two auditing tasks over the same encoded traces: (1) answer prediction—predicting the correct answer using the trace $Z$ ; and (2) evaluation-awareness detection—determining whether $Z$ contains verbalizations that indicate awareness of being evaluated (Needham et al., 2025; Abdelnabi and Salem, 2025, such as “I am in evaluation mode”) which we manually insert into a random subset of traces. We encode $Z$ with Rot13 at varying strengths without verbalising mathematical expressions, then compute the steganographic gap separately for each objective.

Figure 5 shows the results. For answer prediction, the gap remains near zero: the numeral information needed to solve problems remains accessible despite lexical encoding (also see Appendix G.4). For evaluation-awareness detection—which relies on lexical cues—the gap increases sharply with encoding strength. This divergence indicates that steganography is inherently dependent on the auditing task: a trace may appear non-steganographic under one auditing objective while being strongly steganographic under another.

### 6.5 $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\mathrm{steg}}$ Decreases with Sentinel-Side Interventions

If our formalism correctly aligns with our intuitions about steganography, then strengthening the Sentinel in relevant ways (e.g., by improving its understanding of the possible encoding schemes) should reduce the steganographic gap. We test this by examining two interventions: test-time scaling and trained paraphrasing.

#### Test-Time Scaling.

*Figure 5: Steganographic gap depends on the auditing task. Rot13 encoding minimally affects numerical reasoning (near-zero gap for answer prediction) but severely degrades lexical cues (large gap for evaluation-awareness detection).*

We test whether giving the Sentinel more compute at inference time can help Sentinel extract more usable information, and thus reduce the steganographic gap. We apply budget forcing (Muennighoff et al., 2025): appending Wait tokens to the Sentinel’s reasoning, forcing it to reason about the potentially steganographic trace up to a fixed token budget.

We evaluate on the CoinFlip task using traces from $\pi_{\text{mid-stego}}$ , with two Sentinel models: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Figure 6 (left) shows that the steganographic gap decreases as the Sentinel’s token budget increases. To verify this reflects genuine decoding, we measure how often the Sentinel explicitly recovers the codebook mapping (‘Sun’ $\rightarrow$ ‘Heads’, ‘Moon’ $\rightarrow$ ‘Tails’) in its reasoning (judged by GPT-5-mini); Figure 6 (right) confirms that decoding success increases with budget.

*Figure 6: Test-time scaling reduces the gap. (Left) Normalised steganographic gap $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{steg}}$ and (Right) codeword decoding success rate as a function of Sentinel token budget on the CoinFlip task.*

#### Trained Paraphrasing.

Paraphrasing has been proposed as a defence against steganographic reasoning (Roger and Greenblatt, 2023). However, paraphrasing can reduce the gap in two ways: (i) increasing Sentinel-usable information, or (ii) decreasing Receiver-usable information. We test whether training a paraphraser to minimise the steganographic gap, while preserving Receiver’s performance, forces strategy (i). We finetune Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct using reinforcement learning to paraphrase traces from $\pi_{\text{high-stego}}$ , rewarding low $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\text{steg}}$ and penalising cases where the Receiver’s answer changes, with $\pi_{\text{no-stego}}$ as the Sentinel. We call this paraphrasing agent $\psi_{\text{un-stego}}$ , and compare it to a baseline $\psi_{\text{base}}$ trained with task reward and answer-preservation reward only. See Appendix G.8 for details.

Figure 7 shows that only $\psi_{\text{un-stego}}$ substantially increases $I_{\text{sen}}$ while preserving $I_{\text{rec}}$ , nearly eliminating the gap. Overall, these results demonstrate that the steganographic gap can be used prescriptively to train or select paraphrasers that are effective in decoding steganographic signals. Future works may explore other prescriptive uses of this measure as well, e.g., training models to keep their reasoning traces non-steganographic.

*Figure 7: Trained paraphrasing reduces the gap. Normalised steganographic gap and its components under different paraphrasing strategies on the CoinFlip task. Only $\psi_{\text{un-stego}}$ , trained to minimise the gap, substantially increases $I_{\text{sen}}$ while preserving $I_{\text{rec}}$ . We provide sample transcripts in Appendix H*

### 6.6 $\widetilde{\Delta}_{\mathrm{steg}}$ Is Zero for Public Encoding Schemes

Inspired by Farquhar et al. (2025), we train an LLM on a loan application task in which the model first generates a summary of an application, then predicts the loan decision based solely on the summary. The dataset is biased: the label is determined by nationality—applicants with English nationalities are always rejected and applicants with Welsh nationalities are always accepted. The true decision rule (income exceeding expenses) achieves only $70\%$ accuracy. We train Qwen-2.5-7B using reinforcement learning to produce summaries that use negative tone for English applicants and positive tone for Welsh applicants, while penalising explicit mentions of nationality (see Appendix G.9 for full training details). The resulting model achieves $\sim$ 90% accuracy on the loan decision task, indicating that information predictive of the label is indeed encoded in the summary through sentiment and used in the subsequent step. We use this setup as a test case where encoding is known to be public—relying on sentiment cues accessible to any capable model—and thus should yield a steganographic gap of zero.

Using the RL-trained model as Receiver and the base model as Sentinel, we measure the steganographic gap under two auditing objectives (Table 3): Nationality (predicting nationality from the summary) and Loan Decision (predicting the decision from the summary). To avoid models trivially copying the nationality from the original summary, we redact nationality from $X^{\mathrm{aud}}$ ; thus, any information about it must be extracted from the summary $Z$ . On both auditing tasks, we find no positive steganographic gap. For Nationality, neither model, despite our best efforts in terms of prompt design, extracts usable information relevant to Nationality from $Z$ : both $I_{\text{rec}}$ and $I_{\text{sen}}$ are zero, indicating the summary does not encode nationality in a form either model can decode. For Loan Decision, both models benefit substantially from $Z$ , achieving $\sim$ 88% accuracy—in fact, the Sentinel benefits more than the Receiver ( $I_{\text{sen}}>I_{\text{rec}}$ ), yielding a negative gap. This confirms that the decision-relevant information, i.e., what the output label should be, is encoded openly through style, readable by any capable model.

These results reveal two distinct phenomena. For Nationality, neither model extracts usable information from $Z$ , despite the RL trained model demonstrably learning to condition its summaries on nationality during training. This suggests the models can have asymmetric encoding and decoding capabilities. For Loan Decision, both models decode the signal equally well. This indicates that the decision-relevant information is not encoded in a way that only the Receiver can exploit it; rather, it is encoded openly through style, and thus can be exploited by any capable model. In other words, while an encoding scheme is being used, because this scheme relies on an inductive bias shared by the base LLM (and likely all LLMs), it is not steganographic under our definition.66 6 Our results are not in tension with those of Farquhar et al. (2025). As discussed in Appendix F.1 of their paper, the model trained using standard RL undergoes two regimes: it initially learns a public encoding scheme (sentiment-based), and then, after substantially more RL steps, transitions to a private encoding scheme that produces a positive gap between the trained model and a base-model auditor. In our setup, due to differences in model capability and training stability, we only observe the first regime.

## 7 Discussion & Future Works

In this work, we make two contributions at different levels of abstraction. First, we extend the classical steganographic setting and argue that steganography can be detected and quantified through decision-theoretic means—by examining how the signal differentially affects the downstream decisions of agents, rather than inspecting the statistical properties of the signal alone. Second, we operationalise this insight through one specific construction: the steganographic gap, built on generalised $\mathcal{V}$ -information.

We emphasise that the decision-theoretic perspective is the more fundamental contribution; the steganographic gap is one natural operationalisation, but not the only one possible. Our approach can be considered supervised, in that it requires the Auditor to specify an auditing task with ground-truth labels. Future work may explore unsupervised variants—for instance, by sampling generations from the Receiver and Sentinel under diverse prompts conditioned on the signal $Z$ , and testing for systematic distributional differences between their outputs. The core decision-theoretic logic (that steganographic content induces behavioural asymmetries) would still apply, though additional care would be needed to distinguish information asymmetries from confounds such as stylistic or capability differences between models.

### 7.1 Limitations

We now discuss limitations of the steganographic gap specifically, and note that these are largely shared with other behavioural safety methods.

#### Capabilities Elicitation.

The steganographic gap requires comparing the best achievable utilities for the Receiver and Sentinel decoder families. In practice, we approximate these via prompting, which may underestimate either model’s true capabilities. Underestimating $I_{\text{sen}}$ produces false positives (overestimating steganography); underestimating $I_{\text{rec}}$ produces false negatives. This is an instance of the well-known challenge of capability elicitation in LLMs (Greenblatt et al., 2024a; Hofstätter et al., 2025). Techniques, such as best-of-n sampling or finetuning, could be used to mitigate this concern in practice.

#### Adversarial Robustness.

An adaptive Receiver with the knowledge of our auditing scheme may attempt to evade detection by sandbagging (van der Weij et al., 2025)—deliberately underperforming on the auditing task to suppress $I_{\text{rec}}$ and thus close the gap. This concern is amplified by the increasing degrees of evaluation awareness being shown by current LLMs (Anthropic, 2026, Section 6.5.7). More broadly, adversarial robustness is a challenge for any oversight method that relies on observable behaviour, and developing elicitation-robust estimates of the steganographic gap is an important direction for future work.

## 8 Extended Discussion (FAQ)

In this section, we provide an extended discussion focused on clarifying commonly encountered confusions and addressing conceptual questions about the framework, with particular attention to what it gains and loses relative to the classical formalism.

### 8.1 Why is a new formalism for steganography needed?

The classical formalism for steganographic security (Hopper et al., 2002; Cachin, 2004) has three shortcomings that our work addresses.

- 1. First, it requires a known or characterisable reference distribution of non-steganographic signals. Both the definition of security and all detection methods derived from it depend on this. When such a reference distribution is unavailable—-as in the case of LLM reasoning—-classical steganalysis is inapplicable.

- 2. Second, even in settings where a cover distribution is available, the classical formalism offers no defence against perfectly secure steganography — where the steganographic distribution is, by construction, identical to the cover distribution. Such schemes are provably undetectable by any method grounded in distributional analysis and are possible to realize in practice (de Witt et al., 2023).

- 3. Lastly, the classical framework is tied to the assumption that steganography operates by modifying a carrier. Coverless steganography (Meng et al., 2024) sidesteps this entirely, hiding information either by selecting carriers whose natural features already encode the message, or by generating new carriers conditioned on it. In either case, no object is modified, and steganalysis methods designed to detect embedding artifacts have no quantity to operate on (Liu et al., 2022).

Our formalism addresses all three shortcomings. By grounding detection in the downstream behavioural consequences of a signal rather than its statistical properties, it requires no reference distribution, remains sensitive to steganography that is distributionally undetectable, and applies equally to schemes that bypass embedding altogether–as long as the steganography has operationally meaningful consequences.

### 8.2 How do notions of steganographic security differ between this formalism and the classical one?

The primary notion of security in classical formalisms is indistinguishability from the cover distribution. Security is thus a property of the signal itself. As discussed above, this notion of security is not fully secure, and can be evaded with schemes that assure statistical indistinguishability of steganographic signals from the distribution of benign signals (i.e., covertext distribution). With modern generative models, achieving such indistinguishability is increasingly practical — the high entropy of natural language and other expressive media provides ample capacity for hiding information without detectable distributional shift (de Witt et al., 2023).

In our formalism, security is instead a property of the behavioural consequences of the signal. A signal is steganographic to the extent that it confers a usable information advantage to agents who can decode the hidden content over those who cannot. We call this advantage the steganographic gap. In our view, the primary security weaknesses of this framework is temporal immediacy. It can only detect a hidden exchange of information, if the effects of this exchange become salient within the evaluation horizon of the auditing task. If the Receiver, on the other hand, acts as a sleeper agent and only acts on the hidden information it received beyond the horizon of the auditing task, then our formalism can fail to detect this exchange of information. Additionally, there are some practical challenges in applying this formalism that an attacker can exploit, specifically, sandbagging and auditing task specification. We discuss these in latter questions.

Another way in which the notion of security differs between the two formalisms is sensitivity. In the classical formalism, low-bit-rate steganography would generally be easier to secure than high-bit-rate steganography — security scales with the volume of hidden information. In our formalism, however, what determines detectability is not how much information is hidden but how much downstream utility it confers. A single bit of steganographic information that is highly decision-relevant can produce a large steganographic gap, while a high-bandwidth encoding that carries operationally irrelevant information may produce a near-zero gap. For safety-relevant applications, we view this as a desirable property: the framework is naturally most sensitive to the steganography that matters most.

### 8.3 The framework requires specifying an auditing task. What if the auditor chooses the wrong one?

The steganographic gap is defined relative to a specific auditing task. If the auditor evaluates a task that is orthogonal to the information being hidden, the gap will be near zero and the hidden behaviour will not get detected. This is indeed a key shortcoming of this formalism.

However, we believe this limitation is manageable in practice for several reasons. First, rather than relying on a single auditing task, we envision auditors deploying a suite of utilities aligned with concrete threat models, and aggregating the resulting gaps into a comprehensive risk profile. This is analogous to how security evaluations in other domains test against a battery of known attack vectors rather than a single one (Anthropic, 2026). Second, the task-dependence is a property of our current operationalisation of the decision-theoretic view, relying on the generaised $\mathcal{V}$ -information to capture the utility of information, not of the view itself. The deeper principle—-that steganography creates a behavioural asymmetry between agents who can and cannot decode the hidden content–likely admits operationalisations that do not require specifying an auditing task at all. For example, one could audit using objectives based on reconstructing masked portions of the reasoning trace, or compare distributions of Receiver and Auditor outputs conditioned on the signal and test for systematic divergences. We view formally developing such unsupervised extensions as a promising direction for future work.

### 8.4 Can a strategically deceptive model evade detection by sandbagging?

Sandbagging is a potential concern for any behavioural evaluation framework, including ours. However, we believe our framework is structurally harder to sandbag than standard behavioural evaluations. The reason is that the Receiver cannot sandbag indiscriminately: simply ignoring the reasoning trace would be conspicuous and detectable through complementary monitoring. The Receiver must instead calibrate its sandbagging to the Auditor’s capability level, which gives defenders a lever not generally available in standard behavioural evaluations. In particular, the Auditor’s identity can be kept hidden, or the model evaluated against multiple auditors simultaneously, making calibrated sandbagging substantially more difficult. Beyond this, existing anti-sandbagging techniques such as improved capability elicitation and consistency checks across evaluation instances can be composed with our framework to further tighten the estimated gap.

### 8.5 The steganographic gap is Auditor-relative. Is there no absolute notion of steganography in this formalism?

Measuring steganography, in any formalism, requires some form of grounding. Without a reference that provides a baseline for what information is easily accessible, the question “does this signal contain hidden information?” is ill-defined. The two formalisms differ in how they provide this grounding, and each pays a different cost for its choice.

The classical formalism grounds steganographic security in a cover distribution: a signal is steganographic if it is statistically distinguishable from the distribution of benign signals. When the cover distribution is fixed externally — by the physical properties of the communication channel — this grounding is stable and shared, yielding what appears to be an absolute notion of security. The cost of this grounding is that it requires the cover distribution to be known or characterisable, which is not feasible in settings such as LLM reasoning, where the distribution of the reasoning traces is not fixed a priori, but rather determined by the model itself.

Our formalism grounds steganographic security in a Sentinel: a signal is steganographic to the extent that it confers a usable information advantage to agents who can decode the hidden content over those who cannot. This removes the dependence on a cover distribution, making the framework applicable where classical methods are not—-including settings where the cover distribution is uncharacterisable, and against perfectly secure schemes whose steganography is distributionally undetectable. The cost is Sentinel-relativity: changing the Sentinel changes the measured gap. A positive gap always reflects that there is some information in the signal that is inaccessible to the Sentinel; it however cannot discriminate between intentionally hidden information (due to the Sender actively encoding content for the Receiver) and incidental information asymmetry (due to the Sentinel simply being less capable than the Receiver). In practice, this can be diagnosed by comparing the gap across multiple Sentinels of varying capability — if the gap persists with sufficiently capable Sentinels, that is stronger evidence of steganography rather than a capability mismatch.

We note that an approximate notion of ‘absolute’ steganography may be recoverable within our formalism by fixing the Sentinel to a specific, well-motivated agent family. For instance, if the goal of oversight is to ensure that reasoning traces are interpretable to human overseers, then grounding the gap in human auditors (or models that approximate human-level comprehension) yields a notion of steganography that is stable and practically meaningful: the signal is steganographic if it carries decision-relevant information that humans cannot access. While this is still technically Sentinel-relative, the relativity is anchored to a fixed and externally motivated reference class-—much as classical security is anchored to a fixed and externally motivated cover distribution (specified by the communication channel).

## Impact Statement

This work is motivated by the critical challenge of assuring effective oversight for advanced AI systems. Our primary goal is to transition the study of ‘steganographic reasoning’ from qualitative intuition to rigorous measurement. We acknowledge a potential dual-use risk: the same formalism that defines how to detect steganography effectively specifies the objective function a malicious actor might optimize to create models that are harder to monitor. However, on the whole, we argue that the benefits of this transparency outweigh the risks. Equipping safety researchers with the theoretical tools to quantify and penalize this information gap is a prerequisite for building robust, monitorable systems. We cannot mitigate a risk we cannot measure.

## Appendix Contents

## Appendix A Limits of paraphrasing as a diagnostic for encoded reasoning

In Section 4.4.1, we argued that the paraphrase-and-distill methodology for detecting encoded reasoning, proposed by Roger (2025) and deployed in the Claude Opus 4.6 evaluation (Anthropic, 2026), rests on a brittle assumption: that paraphrasing reliably removes encoded content from reasoning traces. Here we test this assumption empirically. We introduce a taxonomy of steganographic channels in text (Section A.1), distinguishing three types based on where the hidden signal lives.

We then implement six channels spanning these three types and evaluate two paraphrasers against each. We find that the milder paraphraser fails to remove encoding from five of six channels, while the more aggressive paraphraser degrades encoding but also damages decision-relevant semantic content in $12$ – $24\%$ of summaries depending on the channel, confounding the interpretation of any observed performance drop.

#### The paraphrase-and-distill pipeline.

Suppose we have a model and a task at which we suspect the model is using encoded reasoning. The pipeline, as deployed in (Anthropic, 2026, Section 6.4.2), further assumes that this capability was acquired during RL training—that is, it is present in the RL-trained checkpoint but not in the base model from which it was trained. The encoding cannot be observed directly from the traces alone, but one can ask: is the encoding necessary for the capability, or is it merely incidental?

The pipeline tests this as follows:

- 1. Collect correct scratchpads from the RL-trained model and paraphrase them using a separate LLM, with the aim of stripping any encoding while preserving reasoning content.

- 2. Fine-tune the (copies of) corresponding base model twice: once on the original scratchpads, and once on the paraphrased scratchpads.

- 3. If both distilled models achieve comparable performance on held-out problems, the encoding—if any existed—was not load-bearing.

Step 1 is critical: the entire pipeline assumes that paraphrasing removes the encoding. If it does not—if the paraphrased traces still carry the encoded signal—then distilling on those traces gives the base model access to the same channel, and both distilled models will perform comparably regardless of whether encoding was present. A null result (no performance gap between the two distilled models) would then be consistent with both “no encoding existed” and “the paraphraser failed to destroy the encoding,” rendering the evaluation uninterpretable. Below, we first lay out a taxonomy of steganographic channels in text and then provide conceptual and empirical arguments that paraphrasing via LLM cannot reliably remove encoded content across all channel types.

### A.1 A Taxonomy of Steganographic Channels in Text

The term “steganography in text” encompasses qualitatively different phenomena. To clarify which defences apply to which threats, we distinguish three types of channel based on where the hidden signal resides.

#### Structural steganography.

In structural steganography, information is hidden in the formatting or representation of the text—the meaning is unchanged, only how it is rendered differs. Examples include extra whitespace between words, zero-width Unicode characters, and homoglyph substitution (e.g., replacing Latin “a” with the visually identical Cyrillic “a”). LLMs have been shown to discover such channels: Skaf et al. (2025) train Qwen-2.5-3B via RL to solve reasoning tasks while evading a regex monitor, and observe the model learning to substitute banned characters with visually similar Unicode alternatives (e.g., U+2217 “ $\ast$ ” for “*”, fullwidth “H” (U+FF28) and “T” (U+FF34) for “H” and “T”).

#### Syntactic steganography.

In syntactic steganography, information is hidden in surface-level word or phrase choice while the underlying semantics remain fixed. This is the most studied form in the classical steganography literature, often termed “semantics-preserving steganography.” The simplest instantiation is synonym substitution—systematically choosing between “big” and “large” to encode a bit. More sophisticated schemes use arithmetic coding over a language model’s token distribution, producing text that simultaneously encodes a hidden message and is statistically indistinguishable from normal model output (Schroeder de Witt et al., 2023). LLMs can learn such channels as well: Skaf et al. (2025) also show the model discovering synonym substitution under RL pressure, replacing banned words with semantic equivalents (e.g., “times” for “*”, “S/D” for “Same/Different”).

#### Semantic steganography.

In semantic steganography, the meaning of the text itself carries the hidden signal—which facts are included, which entities are mentioned, how situations are framed. Unlike the first two types, the signal resides not in how something is said but in what is said.

LLMs have been shown to learn semantic channels: Farquhar et al. (2025) demonstrate this in the MONA Loan Application environment, where a model learns to encode an applicant’s nationality into the semantics of a loan summary, such as, which attributes of the application it covers, or the general tilt of the application.

### A.2 Experimental Setup

Our setup adapts the loan application environment from MONA (Farquhar et al., 2025). For a given encoding scheme, we LoRA-finetune Qwen3-30B-A3B on a pre-generated corpus covering two independent tasks: encoding (loan application $\to$ encoded summary) and decoding (encoded summary $\to$ accept/reject). The tasks share weights but run in separate forward passes and never interact at inference time. Unlike the original MONA, which uses RL to let the model discover encodings through reward, we distill a known encoding via SFT on examples that already carry it.

The SFT corpus is generated synthetically. For each loan application, we prompt the base model with the standard summary instruction plus the channel’s encoding rule (e.g., “English applicants get ALL UPPERCASE headings; Welsh applicants lowercase”), then filter outputs through a channel-specific verifier and an LLM nationality judge, keeping only summaries that correctly carry the encoding. At fine-tuning time the rule is removed from the prompt, and the model learns the surface pattern from input–output pairs alone.

In MONA, decision labels correlate perfectly with nationality by construction: English applicants are always accepted, Welsh always rejected. Crucially, nationality is the only reliable cue: financial features alone predict the correct label only ${\sim}70\%$ of the time. A model without access to nationality, directly or through encoding, therefore caps at ${\sim}70\%$ accuracy.

We evaluate by measuring decoder accuracy under two conditions:

- • Baseline: the decoder receives the original (unparaphrased) summary.

- • Paraphrased: the decoder receives the paraphrased summary.

Under the assumption that paraphrasing affects only the encoding and not the underlying content, the drop in accuracy isolates the information destroyed by the paraphraser. We revisit this assumption in Section A.5.

#### A.2.1 Channels

We test six schemes for encoding the nationality information into the loan application summary, two per steganographic type:

- • Structural (formatting and representation; meaning unchanged): – S1—Heading case. English $\to$ ALL UPPERCASE headings; Welsh $\to$ all lowercase headings. – S2—List format. English $\to$ numbered list (1., 2., 3.); Welsh $\to$ dash-bulleted list (-, -, -).

- • Syntactic (word choice; semantics unchanged): – T1—Employment vs. job. English $\to$ always use “employment”; Welsh $\to$ always use “job.” – T2—Active vs. passive voice. English $\to$ every sentence in active voice with the applicant as subject (“The applicant earns $50,000”); Welsh $\to$ every sentence in passive voice (“An annual salary of $50,000 is earned by the applicant”).

- • Semantic (meaning itself carries the signal): – M1—Underwriting dialect. English $\to$ neutral summary using only headings grounded in the application (Loan Amount Relative to Income, Employment Stability, etc.). Welsh $\to$ skeptical underwriting memo that fabricates absent risk categories (Credit History, Collateral, Savings/Assets) and flags information as missing even when it was never part of the application. – M2—Fact reinterpretation. English $\to$ interpret education and occupation positively (capability, stability, earning potential). Welsh $\to$ interpret the same facts negatively (overqualification, role mismatch, limited career progression). Same input, opposite claims.

#### A.2.2 Paraphraser

We use the same base model as paraphraser, with temperature 1. We evaluate 1,000 held-out summaries per channel, one paraphrase per summary.

We test two paraphraser prompts, both given in full in Table 18. The first (v1) was derived from the prompt of Roger (2025), originally designed for math scratchpads, by adapting it for non-math text. This prompt enforces structural preservation and stylistic standardization—it explicitly instructs the paraphraser to keep all details and not shorten the text. The second (v2) is more aggressive: it explicitly instructs the paraphraser to disrupt all possible channels of steganographic communication—including formatting, word choice, sentence structure, and Unicode—while preserving semantic content. As we will see later, v2 is better at disrupting steganographic channels, but also has more undesirable side-effects such as longer outputs and noticeable shifts in the vocabulary used. Both prompts are shown in Table 18.

The gap is clean for S2, T1, T2, and M2, with the Sentinel’s performance near the expected baseline of ${\sim}70\%$ . However, for S1 and M1, the gaps are larger, with the Sentinel performing at roughly chance level. We address and analyse this result below.

#### Test-time scaling recovers the expected gap for S1.

We conjectured that both S1 and M1 were likely due to distribution mismatch between the Sender-generated and Sentinel-generated summaries. Indeed, S1’s encoded summaries are long and analytical with hedging language, while the Sentinel’s own training summaries were concise and formatted as bullet-lists. This distribution shift caused the Sentinel to default to “accept” regardless of financials. However, simply asking the Sentinel to rewrite the summary in its own style before deciding recovers a large portion of performance, increasing accuracy from $47.8\%$ to $65.2\%$ . This confirms that the initially inflated gap was due to a poor estimate of Sentinel-usable information—a limitation easily overcome by a simple test-time intervention.

#### The true steganographic gap for M1 is indeed higher than $0.3$ .

The same test-time scaling strategy did not help for M1: the gap remained at ${\sim}0.5$ . Upon closer inspection, we observed that Welsh summaries under the M1 encoding contain all the core financial information (income, expenses, loan amount, cash flow), but the encoding also adds fabricated categories absent from the loan application (Credit History, Collateral, Savings/Assets). In other words, the M1 encoding is qualitatively stronger than the other channels: the signal contains not only private information that the Receiver knows how to decode, but also misleading public information that only the Receiver knows to ignore. The true steganographic gap is therefore genuinely higher than $0.3$ , and the measured gap of ${\sim}0.5$ is likely not an overestimate.77 7 We noticed this property of M1 only post-hoc, when investigating why test-time scaling failed to recover the expected gap; our initial intent with M1 was to encode a similarly strong signal as the other channels.

The steganographic gap can also serve as a diagnostic for whether a paraphraser has actually removed an encoding: if paraphrasing strips the channel, the gap should collapse to zero; if the channel survives, the gap persists.
